text: Pathogen: Pseudocercospora angolensis. Symptoms: Dark brown spots (upto 10 mm in diameter) on leaves and fruit, commonly observed with a yellow ring around the spot.; On fruit, these brown spots may turn into raised growths with the yellow halo remaining.; Premature ripening of infected fruit.. Affected parts: leaves, fruit. Spread: Fungal spread across areas, increased by weeds and alternate citrus hosts, reduced by airflow between trees, pruning, plant windbreaks, and reducing overuse of irrigation.. Cultural management: Use of certified, disease-free planting material such as seeds.; Prune trees appropriately to allow airflow between trees and reduce the humidity in the orchard.; Remove weeds and alternate citrus hosts from the orchard and neighbouring areas.; Reduce overuse of irrigation practices.; Plant windbreaks. Preventive advice: Actively monitor orchards for symptoms of infection. Actively collect infected plant parts and fallen fruit and destroy by burning or burying (60 cm deep). Remove young plants from an orchard consisting primarily of mature trees to reduce the ability for disease spread throughout the orchard as young plants are more susceptible to infection. Treatment: No chemical pesticide is registered for this target in the official Tunisian pesticide catalog. Management should rely on cultural and preventive practices only.

text: Pathogen: Phytophthora spp.. Symptoms: gummy substance formation and gum exudation from blisters; rotting roots; cracks and cankers on affected plant parts; necrotic lesions; gum formation on the trunk and branches; root discoloration, yellowing and wilting of young plants. Affected parts: roots, trunk, branches, bark, taproots. Spread: Phytophthora spp. are soil-borne and spread through soil contact and water. Zoospores are motile in water and can be transported through soil water.. Disease cycle: Phytophthora spp. produce sporangia under favorable soil, water and temperature conditions. Sporangia produce motile zoospores in the presence of accessible water. Zoospores encyst, germinate and develop into mycelium. Under unfavorable conditions, chlamydospores are produced and can enter dormancy, later germinating when favorable temperatures return.. Cultural management: choose planting locations away from infected regions; follow sanitary practices in nurseries and greenhouses; avoid collar burying when planting young trees; use soil solarization to reduce soil-borne pathogen inoculum; use clean irrigation water and avoid flood irrigation; keep the trunk dry and provide proper water drainage. Preventive advice: Keep the trunk and collar region dry, avoid contact between the trunk and soil or irrigation water, use clean irrigation water, avoid flood irrigation, and provide proper drainage. Treatment: Registered pesticide treatments in Tunisia: FILAL PLUS WG (active substance: Fosetyl-Al), dosage: 250 g/hl, homologation number: F.051-22, utilization: Foliar spraying; 3 treatments: April, July, October/November.

text: Pathogen: A. alternata. Symptoms: lesions on immature fruit and leaves; induces leaf and fruit drop; produces spots and corky lesions on mature fruit; brown spot on mature Minneola tangelo leaves; leaf spot on rough lemon leaves; symptoms of Mancha foliar on Mexican lime leaves. Affected parts: immature fruit, leaves, mature fruit, fruit, mature leaves, blighted twigs. Spread: conidia dispersed by wind, infect all juvenile tissues of susceptible cultivars when temperature and leaf wetness conditions are favorable. Disease cycle: The disease cycle is simple since there is no teleomorph known for A. alternata. Conidia are produced primarily on the surface of lesions on mature or senescent leaves and on blighted twigs.. Cultural management: planting disease-free nursery stock on wider spacings; pruning tree skirts; reducing irrigation and nitrogen fertilization; breeding resistant varieties (Dancy tangerine, Clementine tangerine); avoidance of overhead irrigation and use of under-tree irrigations systems; wider spacing and skirting of trees. Preventive advice: avoid using susceptible cultivars such as Minneola, Orlando, Nova, Lee, Sunburst, Emperor, Ponkan in breeding programs Treatment: No chemical pesticide is registered for this target in the official Tunisian pesticide catalog. Management should rely on cultural and preventive practices only.

text: Pathogen: Cerotelium fici. Symptoms: yellow spots on top surfaces of leaves, later merging and becoming dark and angular; small raised spots, or pustules, on the lower surface of leaves; pustules also occur on the fruit; leaves yellow and fall; yellowing leaves; leaf drop. Affected parts: leaves, fruit. Spread: spores are splashed short distances from one leaf to another, or between plants; spread over long distances occurs as spores in wind. Disease cycle: A fungal disease with a life cycle that requires water on the leaf surface for germination and infection. Cultural management: Increase air movement in the canopy by regular pruning of branches; Avoid overhead irrigation, instead use trickle tape to apply water at soil level; Do not plant beneath shade, especially in high rainfall areas; Weed to reduce the humidity around the trees; Do not plant in areas that flood or where there is free-standing water after rains; Ensure trees have adequate nutrition with the application of fertilizer or manures so that new healthy leaves will be produced as quickly as possible after defoliation by the rust disease. Preventive advice: It is importance to reduce the time that leaves are wet to stop spore germination and infection Treatment: No chemical pesticide is registered for this target in the official Tunisian pesticide catalog. Management should rely on cultural and preventive practices only.

text: Pathogen: Phomopsis viticola. Symptoms: elongated dark brown to black lesions near the base of shoots, especially on the first 3 to 6 internodes; shoot lesions can coalesce and extend onto the cluster stem; small yellow or light-green leaf spots with dark centers, primarily on lower leaves, which may develop a shot-hole appearance; elongated lesions on petioles can cause leaves to turn yellow and drop; sunken black lesions on rachises can make them brittle and cause cluster breakage; dark, sunken lesions on canes may be visible during dormancy. Affected parts: shoots, leaves, petioles, rachises, canes. Spread: Spores are exuded from pycnidia during wet periods of spring and splash onto young shoots. Disease cycle: Phomopsis viticola overwinters in its vegetative form as well as in pycnidia in the bark or canes. Spores are exuded from the pycnidia during wet periods of spring and infect young green tissues when temperature (40 to 45°F) and moisture conditions (several days of rain) are conducive to infection.. Cultural management: use proper pruning techniques and prune out apparently infected wood; remove dead spurs and pruning stubs from vines; remove prunings from the vineyard and destroy or immediately chop them; avoid planting in low-lying areas where poor air circulation favors infection; use cultural practices that increase air circulation and improve drying; consider hand-pruning instead of mechanical pruning to remove more old wood. Preventive advice: Reduce overwintering inoculum by pruning out infected wood and removing dead spurs and pruning stubs. Remove or destroy prunings and maintain good air circulation and drying within the vineyard. Treatment: Registered pesticide treatments in Tunisia: Sulpex (active substance: Soufre 80%), dosage: 1 Kg/hl, homologation number: F.028-13/23; Agrosoufre (active substance: Soufre 80%), dosage: 1 Kg/hl, homologation number: F.163-11/21; Soufrustulln (active substance: Soufre 80%), dosage: 1 Kg/hl, homologation number: F.031-15/25; TIOSOL 80 (active substance: Soufre 80%), dosage: 1 Kg/hl, homologation number: F.004-14/24; THIOMAX JET (active substance: Soufre 80%), dosage: 1 Kg/hl, homologation number: F.005-20; Microsol (active substance: Soufre 80%), dosage: 1 Kg/hl, homologation number: F.183-11/21; Insuf (active substance: Soufre 80%), dosage: 1 Kg/hl, homologation number: F.200-11/21; MicrothiolSpecial (active substance: Soufre 80%), dosage: 1 Kg/hl, homologation number: F.184-11/21; Kumulus DF (active substance: Soufre 80%), dosage: 1 Kg/hl, homologation number: F.106-11/21; SULFOSTAR DF (active substance: Soufre 80%), dosage: 1 Kg/hl, homologation number: F.54-21.

text: Pathogen: Fusicladium oleaginum (Spilocaea oleaginea). Symptoms: whitish or pale grey circular spots on the upper leaf surface; spots can develop a dark outline, concentric markings or a yellow halo; infected leaves turn yellow before dropping; developing fruit can also be infected under moist weather conditions. Affected parts: leaves, developing fruit. Spread: Spores spread with water splash and with insects such as booklice (Order Psocoptera), which live in leaf litter and on leaves.. Disease cycle: Infection of leaves occurs mostly in winter and spring during wet weather. Infections can remain dormant until autumn if conditions are dry. After periods of wet weather, lesions develop and conidia form on the leaf surface. The spores are then spread by water splash and insects such as booklice.. Cultural management: remove or cover dropped leaves; prune branches to open up canopy to air/sun; grow tolerant olive varieties. text: Pathogen: Phytophthora infestans. Symptoms: black or brown irregular-shaped spots on young leaves that expand rapidly; white cottony growth on the underside of leaves; leaves turn yellow, shrivel and die; dark brown, firm rots on tomato fruit; rapid destruction of tomato plants can occur during severe epidemics. Affected parts: leaves, stems, fruit. Spread: Spores on leaves, stems and fruit are spread by wind or water splash. Wind or wind-driven rain can spread the disease 15–20 km. Long-distance spread is also possible on seed, where the pathogen can be present in the gel around the seed and in the seed coat.. Disease cycle: The life cycle has many fungal-like characteristics. Late blight reproduces in two ways: it can produce sporangia without a sexual process, or two strains can mate and produce thick-walled oospores. Oospores can survive for some time in plant remains or soil and germinate to produce sporangia. Sporangia are produced on leaves, stems and fruit and produce more spores.. text: Pathogen: Septoria lycopersici. Symptoms: spotting; wilting of tomato foliage; circular spots with dark brown margins and tan to gray centers dotted with black pycnidia; narrow yellow halo associated with leaf lesions. Affected parts: tomato foliage. Spread: by splashing water from rain or sprinkler irrigation, overwinters on infected tomato debris or debris of solanaceous weed hosts such as horsenettle, can also survive on equipment such as plant stakes and cages. Disease cycle: overwinters on infected tomato debris or debris of solanaceous weed hosts. Cultural management: rotating for at least 1-2 years between tomato crops; control of susceptible weeds (such as horsenettle) in rotation crops; removal of crop debris from the planting area; careful attention to the timing of irrigation to reduce the length of time during which the plants remain wet; staking plants to improve air circulation and reduce contact between foliage and soil. Treatment: No chemical pesticide is registered for this target in the official Tunisian pesticide catalog. Management should rely on cultural and preventive practices only.

text: [Source: Zymoseptoria tritici] Pathogen: Zymoseptoria tritici. Symptoms: yield loss; infestation in fields planted with wheat susceptible cultivars ranging from 30% to 40%; severe epidemics reducing wheat yields by 35 to 50%; small chlorotic spots on leaves; sunken and grayish-green lesions; light tan lesions with darker colored fruiting bodies. Affected parts: wheat, leaves, glumes, awns, flag leaves, wheat cultivars. Spread: widely distributed throughout the globe, found in Mediterranean region, South Eastern and Eastern Africa, Western Europe, Australia, and North and South Americas. Disease cycle: infection initiated by air-borne ascospores and splash-dispersed conidia produced on residues of previous season’s crop, primary infection occurs soon after seedlings emerge in fall (for winter wheat) or spring, secondary spread within the crop occurs from rain splash by asexual fungal spores, conidia, produced on infected plants, pathogen survives crop-free periods primarily as pseudothecia but also in pycnidia on crop debris, autumn-sown crops and volunteer plants can aid survival over winter. Cultural management: rotation with non-host crops; field sanitation; late planting; inter-cropping of wheat with other crops; planting of resistant cultivars; fungicide application. Preventive advice: long rainless intervals with high temperatures can interrupt disease progress [Source: Septoria tritici] Pathogen: Septoria tritici. Symptoms: black spots between leaves; complete plant death; pale grey to dark brown blotches on the leaves and sometimes on the stem and head; tiny black spots between the blotches; lessions with necrotic margins on the infected leaves; chlorosis of veins in the lower leaves. Cultural management: plant rotation with legumes for at least 1 year; plough deep to expose the innoculum to unfavorable conditions 3 to 4 months before planting; plant wheat in wider rows to help aeration and sunlight penetration to reduce the relative humidity; eradicate volunteer wheat crop as they act as source of innoculum during the off season; avoid over fertilization especially with nitrogen. text: Pathogen: Puccinia striiformis f.sp. tritici. Symptoms: yellow pustules on upper surface of leaf; stripes running along the leaf in older plants; pustules on upper surface of leaves; infection within leaf; spores on inside of glumes, lemma and palea; yellow spores pile up on grain. Affected parts: upper surface of leaf, leaf, leaves, glumes, lemma, palea. Spread: wind spreads spores within crops, and over long distances. Disease cycle: Wheat stripe rust survives year-round on living wheat.. Cultural management: eradicating volunteer wheat growing over summer; sowing varieties with maximum stripe rust resistance; ensuring purity of seed source; treating seed or fertilizer with fungicide for early-sown winter wheats; treating seed or fertilizer with fungicide to delay the onset of stripe rust in susceptible to moderately resistant wheats; monitoring stripe rust activity in your crops.
